newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia says rebels plan to cash in on strike.
newsitem.headline: Colombia says rebels plan to cash in on strike.

text.p: The government said on Tuesday that leftist guerrillas and drug gangs would take advantage of a strike by public sector workers set to begin next week in order to advance their own criminal agendas.

Interior Minister Horacio Serpa denounced the alleged plot after a national security meeting at his office across the street from the presidential palace. Discussion items at the meeting included heavy fighting between leftist rebels and the army just outside the capital, which entered its fifth day on Tuesday.
Intelligence reports indicated that "groups of people working outside the law plan to take advantage of the protest (strike) to create problems," Serpa said.
"Certain drug trafficking groups ... and also guerrillas are interested in stirring things up," he said.
He did not elaborate, but warned the leaders of unions representing about 800,000 workers that support the strike to "very careful" about whose hands they might be playing into.

A Feb. 11 deadline for an indefinite, nationwide work stoppage was set last month in response to the government's plan to hold public sector workers to an average wage hike of no more than 13.5 percent this year, despite inflation of more than 21 percent in 1996.

Newspaper commentators have said the strike marks the first "major confrontation" between the government and organised labour, whose left-leaning leaders provided key support for President Ernesto Samper at the height of Colombia's political crisis last year.

The crisis, which almost forced Samper to resign in disgrace, was prompted by charges that the embattled president knowingly received millions of dollars in drug money to finance his 1994 election campaign.

Serpa stressed in his remarks to reporters that Colombia's union leaders were "responsible people" and said he was not suggesting that organised labour was behind any criminal activity that might coincide with the strike.
He lashed out at the opposition Conservative Party for voicing public support of the strike, however, saying its members were seeking to make "political capital" out of public unrest.
